Trusted Computing verifies that the devices connecting to your phone haven\'t been tampered with. It uses a security chip (TPM) built into the device to prove its identity, similar to how your phone uses fingerprint to prove yours.
When enabled, your phone becomes its own certificate authority - it creates and signs digital ID cards for your devices. When disabled, an external server handles this instead.
An IDevID is like a digital passport for a device. Enabling this means only devices with a verified digital passport can connect. This prevents unauthorized devices from pairing.
Full attestation checks that a device\'s security chip is genuine and its software hasn\'t been modified. This is the strongest form of device verification but requires TPM 2.0 hardware.
When enabled, new devices can pair with your phone on first contact. When disabled, you must manually add each device to the trust store before it can connect.
Attestation proves your security keys are stored in tamper-resistant hardware. This setting controls when your phone requires fingerprint verification before sharing that proof.
Registers xKey as a passkey provider on your device. Apps and websites can then use your hardware-backed keys for passwordless sign-in, just like using a physical security key.

USB HSM mode connects your phone to a computer for hardware security module operations. The ADB-based mode is for development only \u2014 enabling ADB on your phone allows any authorized computer full access to your device. Use Native USB mode for production environments.
Bootstrap methods determine how your phone securely downloads CA certificates when first connecting to a new server. Each method offers different security trade-offs.
Uses special DNS records to verify the CA server\'s identity. Like checking a phone number in a trusted directory before calling.
Uses a pre-shared encryption key to create a secure channel. Both sides must know a shared secret before communicating.
Pins the exact server certificate fingerprint. Your phone will only trust a server whose certificate matches a known fingerprint.
Downloads certificates over standard HTTPS. Relies on the same trust system as your web browser.
Controls whether you need to use your fingerprint or face to approve security operations. Each mode balances security against convenience.

Direct USB connection without ADB. Recommended for production use.
Accept desktop pairing over ADB-forwarded TCP on loopback :8444. For development and emulator testing.
Native USB connects your phone directly to a computer via USB cable without requiring ADB. The phone acts as a USB accessory device. This is the recommended mode for production environments.

TCP pairing lets a desktop connect over an ADB-forwarded TCP socket (loopback port 8444). It is intended for development and automated emulator testing, and is bound to localhost only. All traffic is still protected by the Noise XX handshake.
